title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1
summary: Specifies version 1.1 of the Transport Layer Security protocol, which lets client and server applications communicate in ways designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery. It obsoleted RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0). It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 5246.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS 1.1 lets two applications agree on security settings and then exchange data protected by encryption and an integrity check. It revised TLS 1.0, and later RFC 5246 replaced it.

questions: what is an explicit iv in tls
how does the tls handshake work
subtitle: TLS 1.1 revised the protocol for private and integrity-protected communication between applications.

tldr.problem: Applications communicating over an untrusted network need privacy, message integrity, and a way to negotiate security parameters.
tldr.mechanism: TLS uses a Record Protocol to protect application data and a Handshake Protocol to agree on algorithms and keys and optionally authenticate peers. TLS 1.1 changes the handling of CBC initialization vectors and padding errors from TLS 1.0.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4346 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 5246 and obsoleted RFC 2246.

today: RFC 4346 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 5246. It obsoleted RFC 2246 and was updated by RFC 4366, RFC 4680, RFC 4681, RFC 5746, RFC 6176, RFC 7465, RFC 7507, RFC 7919, and RFC 10015.

sections.title: The Purpose of TLS
sections.content:
TLS aims to provide privacy and data integrity between communicating applications. Its Record Protocol runs over a reliable transport and protects data with symmetric encryption and a keyed message authentication code.

The Handshake Protocol lets the client and server negotiate a shared secret and cryptographic algorithms. It can authenticate peers using public-key cryptography and detects changes to the negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects application data while it travels between two endpoints. The endpoints first negotiate keys and security settings, then use those settings to protect records.

sections.title: Changes from TLS 1.0
sections.content:
TLS 1.1 is a revision of TLS 1.0 with security improvements and clarifications. For CBC block ciphers, it replaces the implicit initialization vector with an explicit one.

It also changes the alert used for padding errors to bad_record_mac, defines IANA registries for protocol parameters, and changes the effect of premature connection closes on session resumption.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.1 changes how CBC records start and how padding errors are reported. It also clarifies protocol details and defines registries for parameters.

sections.title: The Record Protocol
sections.content:
The Record Protocol divides data into fragments, may compress them, adds a message authentication code, encrypts the result, and sends it. A receiver decrypts and checks each record before decompressing and reassembling the data.

A record contains a content type, protocol version, length, and fragment. For CBC block ciphers, each record carries an explicit initialization vector. Sequence numbers are included in integrity calculations to help detect missing, repeated, or reordered records.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS divides application data into records. Each record can be encrypted and checked for changes, and the receiver verifies it before passing the data to the application.

sections.title: The Handshake
sections.content:
The client begins with a ClientHello; the server replies with a ServerHello. These messages select the protocol version, cipher suite, compression method, and session information, and include random values used in key generation.

The server can send a certificate and key-exchange information, and may request a client certificate. The peers then exchange key and completion messages. A resumed session can use an abbreviated handshake instead of repeating the full negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange hello messages to choose security settings. They then establish shared keys, verify the handshake, and begin protected application communication.

sections.title: Alerts and Connection Closure
sections.content:
TLS alerts report warnings or fatal errors. A fatal alert ends the connection. The protocol defines alerts for conditions including an invalid record, an unsuccessful handshake, and an unsupported protocol version.

Each side uses close_notify to indicate that it has finished sending data. This lets the peer distinguish an orderly close from a connection that ended unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: An alert reports a problem and may end the connection. A close_notify message tells the other endpoint that the sender has finished, rather than leaving the end of the data uncertain.
